AFAIK I've never seen a water resistant phone with replaceable batteries.

I agree completely. I feel like a man without a country as far as firearms go; I like them, I think they're fun to shoot. I'll mostly likely buy a few more when the price makes sense and I'd like to go to the range. I am not inherently opposed to firearm control legislation, and I'm deeply upset by the legal and policy roadblocks to doing scientific research into firearm issues.

I'm not opposed to things like background checks on principle. Reading the book Gunfight convinced me we never will or could have an Australian style firearm ban/restriction: too many individual rights of firearm ownership are enshrined in state constitutions.

I'm not convinced by the numbers of the likelihood or effectiveness of a firearm in an home invasion, although I don't fault anyone for wanting one. I think the link between completed suicides and firearms is worth taking an honest look at, although I don't think that means additionally restricting purchases or ownership would be effective as a solution.

I'm not convinced by the data that concealed carry meaningfully reduces crime, but I don't think it has to. In the words of Jim Jeffries, "Fuck off, I like firearms," is a legitimate reason to have them.

I personally don't like the way the NRA argues issues, I find it disingenuous, I understand if people think it's worthwhile for the goal, but it makes it difficult for me to trust their policy proposals. I feel that they are advocates for firearm manufacturers and firearm sales above all else. I think their scaremongering rhetorics about immigrants or foreigners or whatever their ad was 100% bonds them to the GOP.

I may be biased, but I feel the arguments that may sway me more pro firearm rights are the stories of gay men carrying to protect themselves from attacks; I think it's intensely unjust when black men are murdered by the police for lawfully carrying, or even being suspected of doing so. I think it's wild that Ronald Reagan passed sweeping firearm control in response to the Black Panthers, and I think the racist history and motivation of a lot of firearm control would resonate better with liberals and leftists. I think there's a solid amount of left leaning arguments against firearm control that I almost never hear made.

I think directly they're opposed, yes. But an ideologically singular organization that advocated for gun rights and was able to link gun rights for disadvantaged and disenfranchised groups might persuade liberals and leftists while putting forth goals conservatives already agree with.
